Damoy Point lies on the western shore of Wiencke Island, beside Dorian Bay. A rocky shoreline, gentoo penguins and glacier-covered slopes surround a historic wooden hut. Farther up the slope lies the site of a former snow airstrip.

The British Antarctic Survey built the hut in 1975. Polar researchers waited here for flights to Rothera Station when sea ice prevented ships from continuing farther south. The hut and former airstrip are part of Historic Site No. 84; in 2023, the building was restored to its original bright orange colour.

An expedition walk offers views of glacial landscapes and traces of the region's aviation history. The expedition team chooses the landing site and accessible route according to the weather, ice conditions and wildlife. Walking onto the glacier requires appropriate experience and equipment; visits to the historic hut must be arranged in advance.

Danco Island lies in the southern part of the Errera Channel, off the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula. A broad pebble beach stretches along its northern shore. Behind it rises a slope that becomes partly free of snow in summer, while the summit and southern part of the island remain covered in ice.

Gentoo penguins nest on the island, and Weddell seals and crabeater seals may rest along the shore. The British Base O operated here from 1956 to 1959; concrete foundations remain following its dismantling. When a landing is possible, the expedition guides select the group's route with penguin pathways in mind, keeping visitors at a safe distance from wildlife.

Daphne Major rises from the ocean as a dry volcanic cone. The island lies north of Santa Cruz and is made of tuff, rock formed from volcanic ash. From the sea, its slopes and the uneven rim of its crater are clearly visible. Seabirds fly above the rocky shore, and this small patch of land gradually draws the eye.

It was here that Peter and Rosemary Grant studied Darwin's finches for decades. Their observations helped reveal how natural selection operates over several generations of birds. Knowing this history adds meaning to the view of the island: before you is a place where changes in nature were studied year after year.

Access to the island is strictly regulated by the national park, and landing requires a special permit. On a visitor itinerary, Daphne Major is primarily experienced from the water; the exact form of a visit depends on the programme and permissions. The island is especially appealing to those interested in evolution and in discovering the Galápagos through the stories of scientific breakthroughs.

From the sea, Daphne Minor looks like a small, bare volcanic island. Its dive site lies north of Santa Cruz, where rocky and sandy stretches of seabed give way to underwater cliffs.

Reef sharks rest in a small recess in the rock; the usual route passes nearby without entering the cave. Rays, turtles, barracudas and reef fish can be seen in the surrounding waters. Black corals and invertebrates reward a close look along the underwater wall. This is a separate island next to Daphne Major.
